     6	# JITX Substrate Modeler
     7	
     8	Write one Python file holding the substrate. API shapes, units and pitfalls are in the docstrings of `jitx.stackup`, `jitx.via`, `jitx.si`, `jitx.substrate`, `jitx.constraints`, `jitx.inspect`, `jitx.test` and `jitxlib.physics`, and in the JITX docs page [Substrate & Stackup](https://docs.jitx.com/en/latest/essentials/design/substrate.html) (its Vias section: layer indices count conductors only).

313	## 7. Don't pass-through inline-subclass — instantiate
   314	
   315	**Failure pattern.** Using `@inline class stackup(Generic_Stackup): pass` (empty body) inside a `Substrate` instead of `stackup = Generic_Stackup()`. The AI reaches for class-level mechanisms (subclassing, `@inline`) instead of instance composition, then leaves the body empty so the subclass adds nothing.
   316	
   317	**Bad — empty inline subclass:**
   318	```python
   319	class MySubstrate(Substrate):
   320	    @inline
   321	    class stackup(Generic_Stackup):
   322	        pass    # the body is empty — pass-through inline subclass
   323	```
   324	
   325	**Good:**
   326	```python
   327	class MySubstrate(Substrate):
   328	    stackup = Generic_Stackup()
   329	```
   330	
   331	**Note (legitimate inline-subclass case):** `@inline class stackup(Symmetric):` with a *non-empty body* that declares layers is the canonical pattern for defining a stackup. This rule applies only to **pass-through inline subclasses** where the body adds no fields, no overrides, no methods. The discriminator is body content: empty body = bad (instantiate instead); non-empty body = legitimate inline-stackup pattern.

class Tag(builtins.object)
 |  Tags are the fundamental building blocks for design constraints.
 |
 |  Tags are applied to design objects, and are then used by the rule system
 |  to determine which rules apply to which objects.
 |
 |  Tags form a hierarchy through class inheritance, and thus a rule applied
 |  to a tag will apply to all tags that are a subclass of that tag. The name
 |  of a tag is derived from its class name.

decompose(ob, types: 'type | tuple[type, ...] | UnionType', /, *, refs=False, filter: 'Callable[[Any], bool] | None' = None)
    Collect fields of a type or types into a sequence that can be used for
    deconstruction assignment.  The elements are all semi-shallow children,
    traversing lists and dicts, but not other structural elements. Note that
    objects of subtypes can be returned as well.

    Inside an instantiation context, elements of memoized classes (such as
    :py:class:`~jitx.net.Port`, :py:class:`~jitx.via.Via`,
    :py:class:`~jitx.stackup.Material`, pads, landpatterns and symbols), and
    objects reached through such an element, usually come back as proxies (an
    element constructed with unhashable arguments is not memoized and comes
    back unproxied); circuits,
    components, routing structures and plain values such as strings and
    numbers do not. An ``isinstance`` check and attribute access on a proxy
    behave as on the declared object, but ``type(element)`` is the proxy
    class, so reading a class attribute through ``type(element)`` raises
    AttributeError: read it from the element itself, and use
    :py:func:`jitx.proxy.typeof` to get the declared class.
    Each element carries only the fields its own class declares, so when
    ``types`` covers several kinds, a field of one kind raises AttributeError
    on the others (``decompose(stackup, Material)`` returns conductors and
    dielectrics together; decompose by ``Conductor`` or ``Dielectric`` to read
    the fields only one of them declares).

    The classes are declared at module level and the calls run inside a
    :py:class:`jitx.test.TestCase` method or a design build:

Help on function phase_velocity in module jitxlib.physics:

phase_velocity(eps_r: float, mu_r: float = 1.0)
    Compute the Phase Velocity for a specific medium.

    The phase velocity is the signal propagation velocity in a particular
    medium. This function assumes that the medium of propagation is homogeneous.
    For non-homogeneous medium, the user should compute the effective relative permittivity
    and then pass it to this function.

    When a field solver or the fab's impedance report gives an effective
    relative permittivity (eps_eff) for the structure, pass that value. It
    accounts for the real dielectric around the line (layers of different Dk
    and thickness), the conductor thickness and, on microstrip, the line width
    and any soldermask. Without one, these quasi-static closed forms give an
    eps_eff to pass in. In each, ``er`` is the laminate's Dk at the signal
    frequency.

    * Stripline in one dielectric ``er``: the line carries a TEM mode in a
      homogeneous medium, so ``eps_eff = er`` exactly, at any line width.
    * Stripline whose strip lies on the boundary between two dielectrics ``er1``
      and ``er2`` (a prepreg and a core), with equal dielectric height above and
      below the strip: ``eps_eff = (er1 + er2) / 2``. By symmetry the field has
      no component normal to the boundary, so this is exact for a strip of
      negligible thickness. With unequal heights or a thick strip it is an
      approximation, though eps_eff always lies between ``er1`` and ``er2``.
    * Microstrip on a substrate ``er`` with air above: ``eps_eff = (er + 1) / 2``
      is the quasi-static limit for a thin strip as w/h goes to 0, where the
      strip sits on the boundary between two half-spaces, substrate and air,
      and half its field lies in each. Real widths approach that limit slowly,
      because a wider strip puts more of its field in the substrate and
      eps_eff is higher. On ``er = 4.4`` (thin strip, no soldermask), the
      Hammerstad and Jensen (1980) closed form shows this limit overstating
      the velocity by about 4% even at w/h 0.1, 8% at w/h 1, and 11% for a
      50 ohm line (w/h near 1.9, eps_eff near 3.3; a quasi-static
      finite-difference solve also gives about 3.3). Soldermask over the line
      raises eps_eff further.

    Args:
        eps_r: Relative Permittivity of the Medium. This value should be greater than or equal to 1.0
